### Persistent activity can still lose memory accuracy

Location: line 9, anchor `sec:READING-MEMORY`

First content kind: `prose`

Opening passage line: 11
Closing passage line: 15

Paragraphs in source order (complete `PARAGRAPH_REVIEW.json`):

<!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p11 sha256 62e597eb9d3cc6c359ce6fc67ddda9e663386213cb67420a739a9fd4fe2d8692 -->
p11, lines 11-11; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p7; next: p13

> Burak and Fiete (2012) study short-term memory for a continuous quantity, such as a direction or eye angle. A proposed mechanism is that interacting neurons keep activity going after the original input ends. Yet the remembered value can change while the activity persists. The problem is to explain how the properties of the cells and their connections set the rate of this loss of accuracy.

<!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p13 sha256 faecfa341c8fc0b24bb8eff894231fb32aa29457ffdd4dfe2e2ee9df76f7fad7 -->
p13, lines 13-13; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p11; next: p15

> The authors analyze a network with a continuous family of persistent activity patterns, each representing a different value. Each cell sends signals at random times. They use an approximation for small fluctuations to derive how these signals move the stored value, compare the calculation with network simulations, and relate the motion to the best accuracy possible when estimating the stored value from those signals.

<!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p15 sha256 59ac7ccb26e083235272620dc68efd5f23c226b36cec9222f24137ea33985c90 -->
p15, lines 15-15; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p13; next: p19

> Their central result is a lower bound: the uncertainty in reading the network's current value limits how slowly that value can wander. Under the model's assumptions, the variance of the memory error grows with storage time. Reading for longer also has diminishing benefit because the state continues moving during observation. This gives a benchmark for evaluating proposed memory circuits and their recall errors. It applies to the analyzed family of continuous-state memory models, with the required noise assumptions and no external signal anchoring the value. Chapters 3–6 develop the [diffusion calculation](../chapters/ch-memory-dynamics.html), its long-delay behavior, the [information bound](../chapters/ch-memory-information.html), and the limits of [readout](../chapters/ch-memory-readout.html).[^orientation-memory]

### Eye drift points to a shared neural source

Location: line 17, anchor `sec:READING-EYE`

First content kind: `prose`

Opening passage line: 19
Closing passage line: 23

Paragraphs in source order (complete `PARAGRAPH_REVIEW.json`):

<!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p19 sha256 e93e80ea33d4ff1a0588cae92682fa1899dd62394dff2296372f085590eb92ae -->
p19, lines 19-19; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p15; next: p21

> Even while gaze is held on a stationary target, the eyes move smoothly and irregularly between brief, rapid movements. This smooth motion is called [**fixational drift**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}. It changes the image reaching the [**retina**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, the light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye. Understanding its source is therefore part of understanding the visual signals the brain receives. Ben-Shushan and colleagues (2022) ask whether the motion begins mainly in muscles or in neural commands sent to them.

<!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p21 sha256 5530c40e518e38fdbdccbcf5180ae5ed6120bf2272a2eb05161d77496a5aada5 -->
p21, lines 21-21; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p19; next: p23

> They reanalyze recordings from 57 neurons that send commands to eye muscles in two macaques, paired with precise eye-position measurements. They first calibrate the relation between each cell's activity and larger eye movements. They then use it during fixation to compare the movement predicted from one cell with the measured movement. A separate circuit model tests whether a wandering stored eye-position command could explain the movement's amplitude and time dependence.

<!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p23 sha256 0bfe93e919031032888f91408c30269d9f84873f4daaaf2896dc087a64c92387 -->
p23, lines 23-23; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p21; next: p27

> For 350-millisecond intervals, their analysis estimates that about 82% of horizontal displacement variance comes from a common source before the final motor neurons, assuming the fitted movement relation also holds during fixation and the relevant noise contributions do not vary together. This supports a central neural contribution to drift. The memory-circuit model provides a possible explanation of that contribution, linking an internal storage error to observable behavior. The recordings do not uniquely locate the noise inside that memory circuit. Chapters 7–9 separate the [shared-drive inference](../chapters/ch-eye-drift.html), the [timing of drift](../chapters/ch-eye-timing.html), and the [proposed circuit mechanism](../chapters/ch-eye-circuit.html).[^orientation-eye]

<!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p27 sha256 65432e63a8620837f538d3e3163451d95f0dcf7514bdae3df108cababd2cc5b7 -->
p27, lines 27-27; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p23; next: p29

> A [**place cell**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} in the [**hippocampus**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, a brain region involved in memory and navigation, becomes more active in particular locations. Each connected region of elevated activity is a [**place field**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}. Small environments encouraged a picture of one smooth field per cell. Larger environments reveal multiple fields with widely varying sizes and shapes. Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak (2025) ask whether one statistical account can explain this variety across species and spatial dimensions.

<!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p29 sha256 aa56fe28c5ef630ebb8b8df1d603bec472e16ce43a8ce2d733efd11be9e81e28 -->
p29, lines 29-29; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p27; next: p31

> Their model gives each cell a smooth random function of location and allows activity where that function exceeds a threshold. The authors derive predictions for the resulting regions, simulate the model, and compare it with existing rodent and bat recordings from one-, two- and three-dimensional environments. Parameters fitted to field sizes and their spatial arrangement also support further tests of field shapes and connectedness.

<!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p31 sha256 a454cec32b8bafcb32c610ccd91d2b440052a5f475f34105f2b9bd85e27a5c46 -->
p31, lines 31-31; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p29; next: p33

> The model explains different size distributions across dimensions and predicts additional features, such as multiple peaks within a field and inactive holes surrounded by activity. This makes irregular spatial responses quantitatively understandable and supports a common statistical description across the examined settings. Such statistics can arise when cells combine many inputs through largely random connections. The study does not directly measure those connections. Chapters 10–12 develop the [spatial model](../chapters/ch-place-fields.html), its [size and shape predictions](../chapters/ch-place-sizes.html), and the [tests and circuit interpretation](../chapters/ch-place-tests.html). They distinguish exact predictions, limiting approximations and empirical comparisons.[^orientation-place]

<!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p14 sha256 9af80ab1f58efe51f894cfabafef42e4ed696456a693712fb84f3c5ab88882c1 -->
p14, lines 14-14; list_item; priority: unchanged; previous: p13; next: p15

<!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p15 sha256 ea5ea55b56674e27c1ea753925f8e5b1f54af57280f8f51ffa3451e4df5a84ea -->
p15, lines 15-15; list_item; priority: unchanged; previous: p14; next: p16

p3, lines 3-3; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: none; next: p5

> Looking steadily at a small spot does not hold the eye perfectly still. Between brief, rapid movements called [**microsaccades**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, the eye makes a small, smooth, irregular movement called fixational drift. Does this movement begin as noise in the muscles, or does the brain send a changing command to them? Ben-Shushan and colleagues answer this in two stages. Their recordings support a large shared drive upstream of the motor neurons. Their model then proposes a particular source: random motion of the eye position stored in a memory circuit.[^p2-question]

<!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p5 sha256 ca0bc9dead0d4e995e3e496d098a0a1213854eccf928570a5bf5ff1473f4f55a -->

A memory coordinate can diffuse inside a neural network, but the movement produced by that coordinate also depends on the muscles and the mechanics of the eye. We need to follow the signal through those stages before comparing a neural diffusion law with an eye trajectory.

Applying it during fixation then lets us ask whether independent motor noise could explain the observed relationship, and estimate the shared contribution under explicit gain and independence assumptions.

### From stored eye position to muscle action

<!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p11 sha256 ccd80d6128f360a3fe92c364f6d30e0b9ac0a957260418c96f3fd15c30e8a97b -->
p11, lines 11-11; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p7; next: p13

> The eye needs an ongoing command to maintain a position. A brief command to move is therefore insufficient: after the movement, a circuit must maintain activity representing the new position. The [**oculomotor integrator**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is the neural circuit that performs this storage. “Integrator” refers to turning a movement command into a lasting position signal. In the proposed mechanism, the continuous attractor described in the [foundations](ch-persistence.html#sec-foundations-attractor) and [network model](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-spikes) stores horizontal eye position. Noise moves the stored value along that attractor.[^p2-pathway]

<!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p13 sha256 326229916f9e18672b79d20aa5c7df46733a620ecb497ec93a340ebbb62f64d5 -->
p13, lines 13-13; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p11; next: p15

> The signal reaches [**ocular motoneurons (OMNs)**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, neurons whose spikes activate the eye muscles. The recordings came from the [**abducens nucleus**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, a group of brainstem neurons that includes OMNs activating the lateral rectus muscle, which turns the eye outward. Other neurons in that nucleus carry signals to other neurons rather than directly to muscle. The study separated these cell types using their eye movement response parameters. Finally, the muscles and the mechanical properties of the eye, together called the [**ocular plant**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, turn neural activity into movement.[^p2-recordings]

The animals first fixated a stationary target and then tracked a moving target. A wire search coil on one eye measured eye position while an electrode recorded one neuron's spikes. There were 57 identified OMNs. Each recording paired one OMN with eye movement; there were no simultaneous recordings of multiple OMNs. Thus the analysis cannot directly measure the covariance between two recorded motor neurons.[^p2-recordings][^p2-single] p27, lines 27-27; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p25; next: p29 > The initial stationary target was followed by 500–700 ms of required fixation before the target stepped and began moving. Neural voltage was sampled at 25 kHz and eye position at 1 kHz. The authors detected microsaccades using eye speed and acceleration, removed 30 ms on each side of them, and manually checked the remaining segments. For the main displacement analysis, segments shorter than 350 ms were excluded and longer ones were split into nonoverlapping 350 ms pieces. There were 302 such pieces per cell on average, with different counts across cells. These repeated observations improve estimates within two animals; they do not create 57 independent animal samples.[^p2-segments] p29, lines 29-29; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p27; next: p31 > The large movements have a useful role even though the scientific question concerns tiny drifts. > For a centered displacement $Y$ and one centered prediction $X$, the best linear prediction $bX$ minimizes $\operatorname{Var}(Y-bX)$. Differentiating with respect to $b$ gives $b=\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)/\operatorname{Var}(X)$. Its explained fraction of variance is

### Calibrated covariance estimates the common share of movement variance Location: line 199, anchor `sec:EYE-CHI` First content kind: `prose` Opening passage line: 201 Closing passage line: 276 Paragraphs in source order (complete `PARAGRAPH_REVIEW.json`): p201, lines 201-201; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p197; next: p208 > The variance bound establishes that a shared signal exists, but leaves its size open. The next calculation uses the fact that the inverse filter has a calibrated gain in degrees. For one 350 ms interval, write the measured displacement and the single cell prediction as p208, lines 208-208; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p201; next: p210 > where $C=\delta E_C$ is the common upstream contribution, $\eta$ combines motor neuron, muscle, and measurement contributions to measured displacement, and $\epsilon$ is the prediction error from the individual cell. All are displacement variables in degrees. The calculation assumes: p210, lines 210-210; list_item; priority: unchanged; previous: p208; next: p211 > The common contribution enters both signals with unit gain, meaning the same one-for-one displacement scale. p211, lines 211-211; list_item; priority: unchanged; previous: p210; next: p213 > $C,\eta,\epsilon$ are pairwise uncorrelated to the required accuracy. p213, lines 213-213; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p211; next: p222 > Expanding the covariance shows why those assumptions matter: p222, lines 222-222; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p213; next: p229 > The common fraction is therefore estimated by p229, lines 229-229; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p222; next: p231 > These are Eqs. 11–15 in displacement form. The gain assumption requires that the relation calibrated during larger movements still applies during drift. There is also a small covariance between $\epsilon$ and $\eta$, because the recorded neuron's private spikes contribute both to its predictor and to actual eye motion. The paper neglects this contribution as order $1/N_m$ under its many neuron model.[^p2-chi-method] p231, lines 231-231; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p229; next: p239 > Correlation divides the same covariance by a different denominator: p239, lines 239-239; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p231; next: p241 > Large private noise in a cell inflates $\operatorname{Var}(X)$ and makes $R$ small. It need not make the common contribution to the real movement small, because many independent private contributions average down there. p241, lines 241-241; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p239; next: p249 > **Example: correlation 0.17 with a common fraction 0.82.** These numbers are constructed to expose the distinction, not extracted from individual cells. Take independent centered variables with p249, lines 249-249; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p241; next: p256 > Then $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=0.01000$, $\operatorname{Var}(X)=0.23266$, and $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=0.00820$, all in deg$^2$. It follows that p256, lines 256-256; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p249; next: p260 > One cell explains $R^2\simeq2.89\%$ of displacement variance after linear rescaling, while the common signal supplies 82% of actual displacement variance. The larger, poorly predicted part of the single cell signal is private prediction noise. p260, lines 260-260; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p256; next: p264 >
p264, lines 264-264; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p260; next: p266 >
p266, lines 266-266; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p264; next: p268 > Private prediction noise enlarges the denominator of R without changing the covariance. The bars use the same physical scale, so the equal common pieces have equal lengths. See [Shared and private variability, Eqs. 11–15, p. 10](../papers/ben-shushan-2022-fixational-drift.pdf#page=10). p268, lines 268-268; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p266; next: p276 > In the experiment, each cell gives a noisy estimate $\chi_i$, and those estimates can lie outside $[0,1]$. The underlying variance fraction remains in that interval under the model, but the sample covariance need not. The paper estimates each standard error $\Delta\chi_i$ mainly from covariance uncertainty, treating the measured displacement variance in the denominator as comparatively well determined. It then uses inverse variance weighting: p276, lines 276-276; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p268; next: none > To see the weighting, let normalized weights $a_i$ sum to one. Independent errors give variance $\sum_i a_i^2(\Delta\chi_i)^2$ for $\sum_i a_i\chi_i$. Minimizing this subject to $\sum_i a_i=1$ gives $a_i\propto1/(\Delta\chi_i)^2$ and the error above. It does not measure variation across animals or uncertainty in the gain and independence assumptions. ### Independent measurement error adds a constant offset to the MSD Location: line 7, anchor `sec:EYE-MEASUREMENT-NOISE` First content kind: `prose` Opening passage line: 9 Closing passage line: 49 Paragraphs in source order (complete `PARAGRAPH_REVIEW.json`): p9, lines 9-9; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p5; next: p15 > The common variance calculation uses one interval length. To learn what kind of process drives motion, the authors next compare displacements at many time separations. Using the [earlier definition of mean squared displacement](ch-foundations.html#sec-foundations-covariance), p15, lines 15-15; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p9; next: p17 > is the mean squared displacement, or MSD, at lag $\ell$. The data estimate it within each microsaccade free segment, then average the available segment estimates at each lag. Larger lags have fewer eligible segments. The 1 ms sampling sets the available lag spacing.[^p2-msd] p17, lines 17-17; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p15; next: p19 > At short lags, the displacement can be smaller than the search coil's measurement error. Suppose its reading is $E_{\rm obs}(t)=E(t)+\nu(t)$. The measurement error is assumed to have: p19, lines 19-19; list_item; priority: unchanged; previous: p17; next: p20 > Zero mean and variance $\sigma_m^2$. p20, lines 20-20; list_item; priority: unchanged; previous: p19; next: p21 > Independence from true movement. p21, lines 21-21; list_item; priority: unchanged; previous: p20; next: p23 > No correlation between distinct sampled times. p23, lines 23-23; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p21; next: p35 > For a positive lag, p35, lines 35-35; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p23; next: p37 > The mixed movement-error term vanishes by independence. This is Eqs. 18–19. The correction is the variance of a difference of two errors, $2\sigma_m^2$, rather than the variance of a single position error. At exactly zero lag the same error is subtracted from itself, so the MSD is zero. A positive lag plateau near zero lag can still occur when successive measurement errors are independent.[^p2-msd-noise] p37, lines 37-37; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p35; next: p39 > The authors estimated the plateau contribution at order $10^{-3}$ deg$^2$, checked its scale with a coil fixed in space, and subtracted that contribution from the observed MSD. This is a correction of an average statistic, not knowledge of each trial's unknown noise. Smoothing the eye trajectories instead would also change the movement statistics the analysis seeks to measure. If the plateau estimate has uncertainty $10^{-4}$ deg$^2$, a corrected MSD of that size is unreliable even when the plateau itself is much larger. The peer review response uses this example to explain the shortest lag limitation.[^p2-noise-limit] p39, lines 39-39; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p37; next: p41 > For instance, a constructed measured MSD of $0.0014$ deg$^2$ with an estimated noise contribution $0.0010$ deg$^2$ leaves $0.0004$ deg$^2$. A $0.0001$ deg$^2$ uncertainty in the subtraction is already 25% of that result. This is why a corrected short lag point needs an uncertainty assessment as well as a positive value. If measurement errors were temporally correlated, the correction would instead be $2[\sigma_m^2-C_\nu(\ell)]$, where $C_\nu$ is their covariance at lag $\ell$; a constant subtraction would then need revision. p41, lines 41-41; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p39; next: p43 > For a constructed Brownian movement with $D=0.010$ deg$^2$/s, adding independent position measurement errors with $2\sigma_m^2=0.0010$ deg$^2$ shifts every positive-lag MSD upward by the same amount. p43, lines 43-43; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p41; next: p47 >
p47, lines 47-47; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p43; next: p49 >
p49, lines 49-49; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p47; next: p53 > The offset comes from two independent position errors, one at each endpoint. Its removal changes the average MSD; it does not recover each trajectory’s unknown error. The Brownian movement is chosen only to make the constant offset visible. See [Measurement noise correction, Eqs. 18–19, p. 10](../papers/ben-shushan-2022-fixational-drift.pdf#page=10). ### The MSD plateaus for filtered white noise but grows for filtered diffusion Location: line 51, anchor `sec:EYE-FILTERED-MSD` First content kind: `prose` Opening passage line: 53 Closing passage line: 168 Paragraphs in source order (complete `PARAGRAPH_REVIEW.json`): p53, lines 53-53; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p49; next: p60 > The corrected MSD keeps increasing over the observed range, toward a second, while its logarithmic slope decreases and remains between one and two. Define that local slope by p60, lines 60-60; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p53; next: p62 > Ordinary diffusion has $M=2D\ell$ and $\alpha=1$. A roughly constant velocity over a short interval gives displacement $v\ell$ and $M=\mathbb E[v^2]\ell^2$, so $\alpha=2$. Growth faster than linear is called [**superdiffusion**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}. Here it describes a finite range of lags; it does not assert a single power law for arbitrarily long times.[^p2-msd-result] p62, lines 62-62; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p60; next: p68 > Could temporally uncorrelated motor noise acquire the observed MSD just by passing through muscles? A [**low pass filter**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} suppresses rapid input changes relative to slow ones. [**White noise**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} here is an ideal zero mean input whose fluctuations at different times are uncorrelated. In continuous time its strength is defined by an intensity multiplying a delta function, rather than a finite variance at an individual time. A stable, decaying response to this noise produces a [**stationary process**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} in the sense needed here: its mean is constant and its covariance depends only on time separation. Its position variance consequently does not grow with absolute time. Let $E=h*\xi$, where p68, lines 68-68; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p62; next: p75 > The noise intensity $A$ has units input$^2$ times seconds. Expanding the convolution and using the delta function yields, for $\ell\ge0$, p75, lines 75-75; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p68; next: p81 > For a stationary centered position, expanding the squared difference then gives p81, lines 81-81; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p75; next: p83 > If the kernel decays sufficiently rapidly, its overlap with a shifted copy tends to zero. The MSD consequently approaches $2C_E(0)$, a finite plateau. This reconstructs the reasoning of Eqs. 20–22.[^p2-white-noise] p83, lines 83-83; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p81; next: p90 > For the one exponential filter $h(u)=\Theta(u)e^{-u/\tau}/\tau$, p90, lines 90-90; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p83; next: p92 > This simple filter has a short lag MSD proportional to $\ell$ and a long lag plateau. A double exponential filter is smoother at short lags, but still gives a plateau because its kernel also decays. Increasing $A$ raises the curve without removing its flattening. The paper's simulated private OMN noise, passed through muscle dynamics, is both too small and too flat at long lags. In Fig. 3b, using 2,000 heterogeneous OMNs, its contribution is about 1% of the observed variance near 900 ms.[^p2-msd-result] p92, lines 92-92; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p90; next: p94 > Filtered white noise cannot explain continued long-lag growth. Suppose instead the input is a stored position $B(t)$ undergoing Brownian motion with $\mathbb E[(B(t+\ell)-B(t))^2]=2D\ell$. Its position variance accumulates. A low pass filter with nonzero static gain smooths the path while retaining that accumulating long time displacement variance. The following one exponential example is a teaching reconstruction, not the paper's full muscle model. It derives how smooth movement can have a slope between one and two even though the stored position undergoes ordinary diffusion. p94, lines 94-94; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p92; next: p100 > Let p100, lines 100-100; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p94; next: p106 > $W$ is a Brownian process with unit increment variance per unit time, so $D$ has units deg$^2$/s. Define velocity $v=\dot E=(B-E)/\tau$. Taking its increment gives p106, lines 106-106; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p100; next: p108 > Velocity loses its past value over time $\tau$ and receives new random input. To add the surviving effect of those inputs, divide the past into short intervals of width $h$. The Brownian change $\Delta W_j=W(u_j+h)-W(u_j)$ has mean zero and variance $h$. Changes in disjoint intervals are independent. Its contribution to the velocity at time $t$ is approximately $(\sqrt{2D}/\tau)e^{-(t-u_j)/\tau}\Delta W_j$: the initial change has decayed between $u_j$ and $t$. p108, lines 108-108; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p106; next: p114 > The integral against $dW(u)$ denotes the limit of these weighted sums as $h$ tends to zero. It does not require an ordinary derivative of the Brownian path. After the initial velocity has decayed, extending the input history into the distant past gives p114, lines 114-114; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p108; next: p126 > For a lag $s\geq0$, multiply the sums for $v(t)$ and $v(t+s)$ and average. Products of distinct increments have zero mean. The same increment contributes its variance $h$, so the sum becomes an ordinary overlap integral over their shared past: p126, lines 126-126; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p114; next: p137 > Here $r=t-u$ is the age of an input increment. Covariance is even in the lag, so $C_v(s)=(D/\tau)e^{-|s|/\tau}$ for either sign of $s$. Integrating velocity over an interval gives position change. The double integral over its covariance reduces to p137, lines 137-137; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p126; next: p143 > At short lags, $1-e^{-\ell/\tau}=\ell/\tau-\ell^2/(2\tau^2)+\cdots$, so p143, lines 143-143; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p137; next: p149 > The eye keeps approximately the same velocity over that interval. At long lags, p149, lines 149-149; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p143; next: p156 > which grows linearly rather than approaching a plateau. Its local slope is p156, lines 156-156; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p149; next: p158 > approaching two at short lags and one at long lags. At $\ell=\tau$ it is $e-1\simeq1.718$; at $\ell=5\tau$ it is about $1.239$. Thus an intermediate slope can arise from filtering ordinary diffusion, without faster than Brownian accumulation inside the memory circuit. p158, lines 158-158; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p156; next: p160 > The curves compare the two inputs after the same filter with one exponential response, also called a one pole filter. p160, lines 160-160; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p158; next: p164 >
p164, lines 164-164; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p160; next: p166 >
p166, lines 166-166; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p164; next: p168 > The white-input short-lag slope of one belongs to this one-pole example. p168, lines 168-168; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p166; next: none > The actual muscle response contains fast and slow exponential components, and the full model also contains motor neuron filtering and feedback. Those ingredients change the detailed curve. The one exponential derivation teaches the distinction relevant to Fig. 3: a decaying low pass filter of stationary white noise saturates, whereas the same filter, with nonzero static gain, retains accumulating displacement from a wandering position. A slow correlated peripheral source is a different hypothesis from the temporally uncorrelated noise rejected by this comparison. ### A noisy integrator can reproduce drift after muscle filtering

Location: line 7, anchor `sec:EYE-CIRCUIT-MODEL`

First content kind: `prose`

Opening passage line: 9
Closing passage line: 85

Paragraphs in source order (complete `PARAGRAPH_REVIEW.json`):

<!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p9 sha256 eacb0612bb83ad26dc3c1da2b1afeda1529552493d67197223a2d90d0c15fee9 -->
p9, lines 9-9; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p5; next: p11

> The recording analysis places much of the drive upstream of OMNs. To test whether integrator noise could supply it, the authors build a model from a noisy memory circuit through to the eye. The model adapts an earlier goldfish integrator architecture to primate tuning and variability. There are two populations, with excitation within each and inhibition between them. Their firing increases for opposite directions of gaze. This supplies the recurrent interaction needed to maintain a range of stored positions.[^p2-network]

<!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p11 sha256 2c55ee2c6b6164e165046b3628b1610bb123b45dafe2dc76be02dc1cdcf2a568 -->
p11, lines 11-11; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p9; next: p18

> For the right population, the model's rate is

<!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p18 sha256 670a618c0d9e32cdfcced57c0ccebb39ddc8097dbe087aa1f4cefc79375840e2 -->
p18, lines 18-18; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p11; next: p20

> $E_{OI}$ is the internally represented position in degrees, $\zeta_i^R$ is a tuning slope in spikes/(s deg), and $\lambda_i^0$ is a rate offset in spikes/s. Taking the maximum with zero prevents negative firing. $F$ is a feedback input in degrees, defined below. The matching left neuron has the opposite slope, $\zeta_i^L=-\zeta_i^R$. In an active neuron, a change of one degree changes its rate by $\zeta_i$.

<!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p20 sha256 0fefbab2856e1562ae4a490a06ce94073bb6cf614e00e721593ea1af74d60be4 -->
p20, lines 20-20; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p18; next: p28

> Spikes produce synaptic activity according to

<!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p28 sha256 af7902f51d056f623d1f9e3bfe92c3cd163f3085baba4c42d920c06b2e517fc8 -->
p28, lines 28-28; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p20; next: p30

> Here $\xi_i^R$ is a spike train generated at rate $\lambda_i^R$, $\tau_s$ is the synaptic decay time, and $\lambda_t=60$ Hz sets the rate scale in the nonlinear synaptic response. Treating spikes as counts, $X_i$ and $S_i$ are dimensionless, and the weights $\eta_i$ are in degrees. Between spikes, $S_i$ decays exponentially; one spike adds a jump of $1/[\tau_s(\lambda_t+\lambda_i^R)]$. Replacing spikes by their mean rate gives a drive $\lambda_i^R/(\lambda_t+\lambda_i^R)$ that approaches one as the rate increases. This is the model's saturating synaptic effect, rather than the purely linear synapses of the basic 2012 example.[^p2-network]

<!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p30 sha256 644dd42008e965323f60d3c11968b02f946c0972597764d6e0a09d713b40cf1a -->
p30, lines 30-30; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p28; next: p38

> The readout $E_{OI}$ feeds back into the rates, so these equations define a recurrent network. Persistence requires a further condition on that feedback. Set $F=0$ and replace spikes by their mean rates. Define the mean saturated drives at a proposed stored value $z$ by

<!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p38 sha256 4e85e73974ec9b54a93f3b2d6ada8057939635f18aab8c0a679c6ecf72ab1cf3 -->
p38, lines 38-38; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p30; next: p46

> Multiply each synaptic equation by its readout weight, subtract the left contribution, and sum. Since the same $\tau_s$ applies to every unit, the readout obeys

<!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p46 sha256 e6a2513f8858d08feee8803fd608767f0d15c0c1779cf42a9163cb098060ee08 -->
p46, lines 46-46; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p38; next: p53

> An exact continuum of persistent readout values would require $G(z)=z$ over the represented range. For a small displacement from a fixed value, Taylor expansion gives

<!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p53 sha256 3d4fd9a575f1c0417e726edf74b09503c18f6a1002aa184352294f17464a8fd7 -->
p53, lines 53-53; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p46; next: p55

> Thus $G'(z)=1$ is the local neutral condition for the stored coordinate. Stable directions of the remaining synaptic state are also needed for an attractor. The weights were optimized to approximate the fixed-point relation across $-50$ to $50$ degrees. Residual mismatch can produce deterministic drift, so this finite optimized circuit provides approximate persistence rather than an exactly neutral continuum. The tuning slopes and thresholds were sampled to match reported macaque relationships and variation. With spikes, perturbations along the nearly neutral direction additionally accumulate. This reduction is a teaching derivation from the paper's equations; Figure 4 separates the resulting internal diffusion from later muscle smoothing.[^p2-network]

<!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p55 sha256 bec9b956b359fac96d7d94ee37835ffd88b40ba3cfc1da3207f747ad35d26ab5 -->
p55, lines 55-55; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p53; next: p63

> The motor neurons receive this position signal:

<!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p63 sha256 dc789f13c057db91a7975ce8b20dae47a49a8bfc0a45404054f3ebe109469778 -->
p63, lines 63-63; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p55; next: p65

> $\lambda_i^M$ is a motor rate in spikes/s, $E_{T_i}$ is that neuron's position threshold in degrees, and $k_i$ is its position sensitivity. $\xi_i^M$ is its generated spike train. The filtered output $s_i^M$ also has units spikes/s, with decay time $\tau_{MN}$. One spike makes a jump of $1/\tau_{MN}$; at constant mean rate, the mean output is that rate.

<!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p65 sha256 ddcb220d0dfb7202998c334244af8f386a828df6a8544acf98825fc373b6d8b8 -->
p65, lines 65-65; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p63; next: p72

> Each motor unit's muscle and plant response is represented by a position contribution $E_i$ satisfying

<!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p72 sha256 3c2d953faf07527bf3bcdf292f35e5db291ea8ddb0a0835a7b880a1c398e068f -->
p72, lines 72-72; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p65; next: p74

> These are Eqs. 28–31. The second order equation uses the same roles and units as the forward fit. At constant $E_{OI}$, an active unit has mean $s_i^M=k_i(E_{OI}-E_{T_i})$, giving mean $E_i=E_{OI}$ when derivatives vanish. Averaging therefore transmits the common position while reducing independent private fluctuations. This is an effective model of combined motor output, not a claim that one motor unit moves an isolated eye of its own.[^p2-motor]

<!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p74 sha256 136a8be33cc7785e4a5baecf0bb1832cea6b8f9f8a858e32423042a32d9d832c -->
p74, lines 74-74; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p72; next: p76

> The model used diverse thresholds and response coefficients, with motor thresholds sampled between $-45$ and $-5$ degrees, and imposed $m_i<r_i^2/(4k_i)$ to give nonoscillatory individual response kernels. Main Methods report $N=30{,}000$ integrator neurons, $N_m=1{,}000$ OMNs, and $\tau_s=20$ ms for the main full simulation. The separate private OMN comparison in Fig. 3 used 2,000 OMNs. These neuron counts belong to different simulation comparisons.[^p2-motor]

<!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p76 sha256 8f07618e944efcd34835f24a99793429fdb45a9eb8f0aa016cb6bd2a12d40534 -->
p76, lines 76-76; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p74; next: p83

> The final loop is delayed visual feedback:

<!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p83 sha256 157ca33f74a870b3a44e71a52b201d3d89c57dbdd45a3120e4fe723a47144f6f -->
p83, lines 83-83; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p76; next: p85

> Both positions are in degrees, so $A$ is dimensionless in this formulation. The main value is $A=0.015$. If gaze and its internal representation have recently moved rightward, the delayed position is to their left, making $F$ negative. Its contribution to the integrator rates then opposes continued rightward movement. The difference can serve as an estimate of recent movement; it is not an error relative to a fixed absolute target position. For a slowly varying position that the eye tracks, $E(t-\tau_d)-E_{OI}(t)\simeq-\tau_d\dot E(t)$, showing the velocity-like action and sign. The approximation requires tracking and slow change over the delay.[^p2-feedback]

<!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p85 sha256 c748cf8e7e32992c2f33cde2c252ae4998dccb11b1ef9cadf3a0c76263e78fcd -->
p85, lines 85-85; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p83; next: p89

> The effect on the ongoing MSD must be checked from the coupled model, rather than inferred from the delay alone. A short MSD lag is a separation between two samples in a running process, not the time since a new perturbation. Past measurements can already affect both samples, and $F$ also contains the immediate term $-A E_{OI}(t)$. Extended Data Fig. 3 compares the model with and without feedback: feedback changes amplitude across lags, while its larger effect on logarithmic slope occurs at longer lags. Figure 5 shows the full model. Muscle filtering supplies the short-lag smoothness, and feedback improves the detailed longer-lag fit. These are results of this model comparison, not a hard delay-based cutoff or a claim excluding visual control under other tasks.[^p2-feedback]

> An agreement in amplitude is informative only if we know how much freedom the model has. The paper uses regular spike trains. The [spike variability section](ch-foundations.html#sec-foundations-poisson) defined the interspike interval coefficient of variation (CV) as the interval standard deviation divided by its mean. A Poisson process at constant rate has CV one; the model uses about 0.22 for integrator neurons and about 0.07 for OMNs. Such firing is called [**sub-Poisson spiking**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} here because its long window count variability is lower than a Poisson process at the same rate, under the interval construction used in the model.[^p2-cv]

<!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p91 sha256 426484c85a1fa9facac2aadc3757571dcf77e291c22e7490984488a5dad39d4f -->
p91, lines 91-91; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p89; next: p93

> The construction starts with a Poisson process at $M$ times the desired rate and retains every $M$th spike. At constant rate, a retained interval is the sum of $M$ independent exponential intervals. Each initial interval has mean $1/(M\lambda)$ and variance $1/(M\lambda)^2$. The retained interval therefore has mean $1/\lambda$, variance $1/(M\lambda^2)$, and CV $1/\sqrt M$. This preserves the mean rate while reducing variability. Its use at changing rates is part of the model; the simple interval derivation assumes a constant rate.

<!-- pedagogy-paragraph: p93 sha256 1c34aa437a2473f6ff12b4d03a98c480e59c43356f8cf27507f3da19fe1cf438 -->
p93, lines 93-93; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p91; next: p101

> At constant rate, the retained intervals are independent. This is a [**renewal process**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, a spike process whose successive intervals are independent and identically distributed. Let their mean be $\mu=1/\lambda$ and standard deviation $\sigma_I$. The time to $n$ spikes has variance $n\sigma_I^2$. For a long fixed window $L\simeq n\mu$, a fluctuation in total interval time produces the opposite fluctuation in count divided by $\mu$. Thus

p101, lines 101-101; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p93; next: p103

> This explains why the diffusion scale contains CV squared: it is the strength of the accumulated spike fluctuations relative to the Poisson case. The [diffusion calculation](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-diffusion) and [information bound](ch-memory-information.html#sec-memory-bound) show how projecting those fluctuations onto a neutral memory direction adds a factor proportional to $1/\tau_s^2$ and, for a comparable independent population, $1/N$.

> If instead sensitivity is expressed as the fractional slope $b=a/\lambda_0$, in inverse degrees, the same expression becomes

> This second form has the dependence printed in the paper's Eq. 1, $D\propto\mathrm{CV}^2N^{-1}\lambda_0^{-1}k_0^{-2}\tau_s^{-2}$. p151, lines 151-151; prose; priority: unchanged; previous: p142; next: p155

## ch:PLACE-FIELDS - Field counts and gaps reveal threshold and scale

Source file: `content/chapters/05-place-fields.md`

Purpose: A cell recorded on a short track may have one smooth firing hill. On a long track, the same kind of cell may have several separated fields, each with a different width and height. In a room, its active regions can bend, split, and surround inactive holes. How could one model produce this variety and still make useful predictions?

Sidecar sections: Thresholding a smooth Gaussian input produces place fields, Upcrossings count fields, with an endpoint correction, Mean field and gap lengths separate threshold from scale
